items.stem: Write an essay of about 150 words on the following topic: your university wants to increase the recycling rate in dormitories. Suggest one practical measure and explain why it should work.

answer.text: Instead of printing more instructions, the university should publish a weekly ranking of dormitory buildings by recycling rate. Each building would see its own figure and its position among neighbours. The measure is cheap, since the data are already collected when the waste is weighed, and it works on a well-documented principle: people adjust their behaviour when they can see how it compares with that of people around them. To avoid resentment, the ranking should praise improvement rather than shame the bottom building, and the top three could receive a small fund for a floor party. Visible progress, rather than another leaflet, is what changes habits.

answer.text: Older adults are not short of motivation: they enroll in online courses in large numbers. What they lack is support in the first hours, when a confusing menu or a failed upload can end the attempt. Universities could therefore offer a short induction, either in person or by phone, in which a student helper sits beside the learner and completes one real task together. Platforms could simplify registration and keep a telephone line open during the first week. Neither measure is expensive, and both attack the real barrier, which is learning the technology alone rather than learning the subject. Completion, not enrolment, is the number that matters.

answer.text: Bike-sharing schemes usually start with crowded streets and end with rows of broken bicycles. The novelty explains the early peak; the flat line afterwards has more ordinary causes. answer.text: Students often assume that only internships count when employers read a CV. Recruiters tell a more nuanced story. Volunteering is seldom a formal requirement, but interviews are built around questions about teamwork and problem solving, and a term spent running a food bank shift answers those questions better than a month of photocopying. What matters is not the label of the activity but the evidence it supplies: reliability, coordination, persistence. Students should therefore choose activities by the responsibilities they involve rather than by the prestige of the organisation. A well-documented volunteering role can be worth more than a famous name on a certificate.

answer.text: Wellness programmes are popular because they are visible and inexpensive. A gym discount and a step counter signal that the company cares, yet the evidence suggests they reach the wrong people: participation is highest among employees who are already fit, and the measured gains are small. The main sources of stress lie elsewhere, in long and unpredictable hours, low control over tasks and unclear expectations. No app offsets a schedule that changes without notice. The more effective investment is therefore organisational: publish shifts in advance, let teams influence how work is divided, and make priorities explicit. Health programmes can supplement such changes, but they cannot substitute for them.

items.stem: Write an essay of about 150 words on the following topic: some tourist towns now charge an entry fee or limit visitor numbers. Discuss whether such measures are justified.

answer.text: Tourism brings income, but it also raises rents, replaces local shops with souvenir stalls and pushes residents out. An entry fee or a daily limit on visitors looks unwelcoming, yet it addresses a real problem: the town must remain liveable for the people who work there. The revenue can be used to maintain the streets and facilities that visitors come to see, which is precisely what a crowded destination struggles to fund. Such measures are not against tourism; they protect its foundation. The design matters, however: fees should be modest, revenue should be visible in local upkeep, and residents should not be charged for their own town.
